answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
Consequential accounting is the only way to measure impact of corporate actions and will add significant value as it will encourage corporations to act. The GHGP has long recognized the need for BOTH inventory (attributional) accounting and impact (consequential) accounting. These report different elements which, taken together, provide the full picture to drive maximum climate impact. GHGP has specifically stated that attributional methods are only for inventory purposes. Thus, without consequential, there is no measurement of action and what gets measured is what will be done.
Unfortunately, the approach proposed by the GHGP in this consultation document does not achieve the above objectives, in part due to its use of the Project Protocol, an optional and little used protocol that is not used by target setting bodies or reflected in any of the regulatory uses of Scope 2 (Eu and California). It is important that consequential be equal to MBM and that there be a net number to drive action that will be reflected in the regulatory uses.

Benefits.
The primary benefit of consequential accounting is that it is the only framework capable of measuring impact, rather than attribution. A consequential approach based on marginal emissions can provide decision-useful information to guide procurement, investment, and policy toward actions and locations with the greatest emissions-reduction potential. By reflecting real grid operations, including congestion and emissions data, consequential metrics can improve alignment between corporate actions and actual decarbonization outcomes and encourage corporations to take the most meaningful actions. Importantly, in this political environment, McKensey has found using consequential marginal emissions will lower consumer cost compared to the GHGP proposed MBM approach.[1]

Challenges.
To be meaningful, consequential accounting must quantify net system impact, including both emissions avoided through generation and emissions induced by electricity consumption. Avoided-emissions-only approaches are incomplete and risk overstating benefits. Another challenge is ensuring consequential metrics are used alongside inventories rather than treated as optional or informational; otherwise, they are unlikely to influence decisions. Data availability and quality also vary across regions, particularly for high-frequency marginal emissions data, which argues for flexibility and transparency rather than rigid requirements.

Unintended consequences.
If consequential accounting is designed to mirror project accounting or coupled with stringent additionality or deliverability requirements, it risks undermining its own objectives. Overly restrictive frameworks can raise costs, reduce participation in voluntary procurement, fragment demand, and shift buyers away from long-term, financeable contracts toward lower-impact compliance instruments. These outcomes would likely reduce aggregate emissions reductions rather than increase them. Similarly, mandating excessive temporal or spatial granularity where data quality is weak can reduce comparability and force reliance on estimates, eroding confidence in reported results.

Practical considerations.
Effective consequential accounting should prioritize transparency, scalability, and comparability. Methods should rely on observable system behavior and available market data, align with annual reporting cycles, and avoid speculative counterfactual tests that cannot be consistently applied or audited like additionality. Consequential metrics should inform decisions and investment signals, not function as a gatekeeping mechanism that limits participation without delivering demonstrable emissions benefits.
[1] McKinsey& Company, Rethinking you company’s clean-power strategy, February 2025.
https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/electric-power-and-natural-gas/our-insights/rethinking-your-companys-clean-power-strategy#/

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
The proposed formula is incomplete because it quantifies avoided emissions from procurement without also quantifying induced emissions from electricity consumption. By excluding induced emissions, the proposed formula cannot distinguish between actions that reduce total system emissions and those that simply shift emissions. A net-impact framework that includes both consumption and generation effects is essential to be useful for decisions and impact accounting.

Both the consequential framework and analysis demonstrate that avoided-emissions-only formulations systematically overstate impact when consumption-induced emissions are ignored. The formula as provided does not achieve what is needed for Impact Accounting to be useful to reporting entities. This is primarily because it is currently only applicable to emissions avoided by procurement and does not calculate or allow emissions caused by consumption. The ability to calculate emissions caused AND avoided is a pre-requisite for the impact accounting option to have any material utility for reporting entities. [1],[2]

It should also be noted that it is my understanding that this formula does not represent what the TWG consequential subgroup proposed, which includes emissions from consumption.[3] The draft response highlights that the TWG subgroup originally advanced a net-impact formulation, and that the avoided-only structure reflected in the consultation materials aligns more closely with legacy project accounting that has seen limited real-world uptake. In addition, target-setting bodies cannot rely on avoided-only metrics because they lack a defined counterfactual baseline tied to actual consumption.

Finally, it has been shown that net system emissions can increase even when procurement appears beneficial on an avoided-only basis, particularly in congested regions.

[1] WattTime: Accounting for Impact, https://watttime.org/wpcontent/uploads/2023/12/WattTime-AccountingForImpact-202209-vFinal2.pdf
[2] RE-Source: Carbon Matching, https://www.emissionsfirst.com/ _files/ugd/820a9e_23bdd35c3c65419a9501ceaf32cc1d40.pdf
[3] Public Statement from Members of the GHG Protocol Scope 2 TWG Consequential Subgroup, November 2025, https://marginalimpactmethod.org/

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text: No, consequential accounting should focus on primary marginal effects to maintain clarity, comparability, and feasibility.

answers.label: Why secondary effects should be excluded
answers.text: Secondary effects introduce speculative assumptions, reduce transparency, and materially increase modeling complexity without improving decision usefulness.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text:
If we agree that the purpose of consequential accounting in this context is to measure routine impacts because of consumption and generation to inform target setting, consequential metrics must be reported annually, consistent with inventory accounting and measuring progress against targets.

The grid mix is dynamic, so reporting consumption and generation at least annually should be required to capture their routine impacts that inform purchasing decisions and capture progress toward targets. The scientific integrity of this method will be improved if this metric changes over time as the grid evolves (becomes more/less clean, improves transmission, etc.) rather than relying on a one-time forecast which has a high degree of uncertainty and risks gamesmanship in the forecasting methodology.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
I do not support imposing an additionality requirement on consequential accounting or on Scope 2 Market-Based Method (MBM) reporting. Scope 2 is, and has always been, an attributional framework, not a causal or project-finance test. Introducing mandatory additionality would represent a fundamental departure from established GHG Protocol practice and would undermine the voluntary procurement mechanisms that have driven a substantial share of new clean energy deployment. [CEBA] [1]

There is no empirical evidence that additionality tests are correlated with greater real-world emissions reductions. Additionality assumes that projects would be built regardless of PPA’s or REC’s which current market conditions show are not true. In practice, nearly all new utility-scale renewable projects require long-term contracts or REC revenue certainty to reach financial close. As a result, the existence of a buyer is itself the causal mechanism enabling build, making ex ante additionality tests redundant and misleading.[2]

Ironically, the studies that support additionality are based on capacity-expansion models that optimizes the cost based on a weighted average cost of capital calibrated to historically contracted or policy-supported revenue, not merchant risk while also assuming a 30-year economic life, implying that some form of long-term revenue certainty (e.g., PPAs, policy-backed REC value, or equivalent mechanisms) must exist over that horizon for the modeled build-out to be financeable in practice [5]. Thus, the studies themselves contradict the need for additionality and yet again fail the scientific integrity criteria.

Additionality assessments for renewable energy credits (RECs) often relied on simplified assumptions about REC prices and their impact on project finance, but many studies explicitly acknowledge the lack of granular data on actual REC values and investor-level financial considerations. For example, Ever.green notes that “without detailed investor-level pricing and contract data, it is challenging to quantify how REC revenue affects financing feasibility and risk premiums”[4].

Finally, mandating additionality would raise the cost of capital by penalizing investors in existing plants, fragment procurement into smaller and less bankable transactions, and shift buyers away from high-impact long-term PPAs toward short-term compliance instruments. By steering procurement toward “additional” projects in the easiest-to-build areas, additionality requirements can unintentionally concentrate new renewable development in the same locations, increasing transmission congestion, curtailment, and local grid constraints rather than reducing system-wide emissions.

If additionality is required, any test should be simple and easy to calculate using available information. Of the test, the regulatory test would make the most sense. To address the concern of low-cost recs, requiring the REC price divided by the average 24-hour price to exceed a minimum level of say 15% would be simple to use and easily understood. More complex tests are likely to limit future corporate procurements.

[1] https://cebuyers.org/wp-
content/uploads/2025/09/CEBA-Report-Corporate-Demand-Drives-Clean-Energy.pdf
[2] Groobey, Pierce, Faber and Broome, Project Finance Primer for Renewable Energy and Clean Tech Projects, Wilson Sonsini, July 2024 https://www.wsgr.com/PDFSearch/ctp_guide.pdf
[3] Xu, Q., Jenkins, J.D. et al. (2024). System-level impacts of voluntary carbon-free electricity procurement strategies – supplemental materials, pg 2 referencing NREL ATB 2021 Joule, 8(2), 374–400. https://www.cell.com/joule/fulltext/S2542-4351(23)00499-3 and https://atb.nrel.gov/electricity/2021/financial_cases_&_methods (which specifically refers to favorable financing for long term contracts)
[4] Ever.green, “Methodology for Additionality in REC Markets,” 2023, https://www.ever.green/insight/evergreen-methodology-recs-with-additionality

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text:
Any tests that rely on confidential data and subjective assumptions, making them impractical and non-comparable across entities. For example, as drafted, the timing, barrier, performance standard, contractual and the financial analysis test depend on confidential project pro formas and assumptions about investor behavior that cannot be standardized or audited. The common practice test and even regulatory tests vary widely across jurisdictions, reinforcing the need for optional rather than mandatory application.

It is also important to avoid too strict of test so as not to limit procurement. Given increasing demand for power and for natural gas turbines (sold out into 2029 or 2030), making it more difficult for companies to benefit from achieving targets of using renewables is a giant step in the wrong direction for a planet that is already facing hostile U.S. government policies.

To address the concern of low-cost recs, requiring the REC price divided by the average 24-hour price to exceed a minimum level of say 15% would be simple to use and easily understood test.

answers.label: Additionality tests missing from the framework
answers.text: To address the concern of low-cost recs, requiring the REC price divided by the average 24-hour price to exceed a minimum level of say 15% of the average 24-hour price would be simple to use and easily understood test and assure that the REC price is meaningful to both the purchaser and the project financials.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text:
Operating margin methods should reflect time- and location-specific dispatch effects using available ISO and market data.

A preferred waterfall for operating margin methodologies is b. SCED - locational, a. SCED - fuel on the margin, then e. Statistical. These models are most accurate for the following reasons:

- Observable data: Using observed data, rather than model, allows for increased accuracy within the model. I align with suggestions from the ZeroGrid Impact Advisory Initiative, which specify the need for a standardized approach with observable data to limit confusion and manipulation [1].

Methods that are purpose-built to leverage data from system operators are generally considered significantly more accurate for estimating the immediate operational impacts of actions [3].

- Use of Marginal Emissions Rates: According to research, marginal emissions rates provide the highest level of precision, as average emissions rates introduce inaccuracies. Ex. from the VERACI-T group: "We evaluate multiple prevalent existing MEF models and find that both dispatch and statistical MEF models have a high degree of agreement with the benchmark MEF, while heat rate and average emissions do not." [2]

- Attention to transmission congestion: Locational SCED models generate highly granular marginal emissions rates, measured at a specific location, which is key for measuring impacts of congestion. In a recent study conducted by Johns Hopkins University and REsurety, marginal emission rate estimates were calculated using a nodal dispatch model (like a locational SCED simulation) for ERCOT, based on marginal generator data and nodal LMP, were validated in a study comparing marginal emissions datasets, in which it was found to be the most accurate dataset. [3]

- Simpler to use: For improved feasibility, I agree with ZeroGrid IAI's view that the model should also be simpler to use. Models requiring individual inputs risk modifying the model, and has the potential to "improperly inflate the estimated impact of their actions" [1]

[1] ZEROgrid’s Impact Advisory Initiative’s Performance Metric Principles , https://zerogrid.org/wp- content/uploads/dlm_uploads/2025/05/iai-performance-metric-principles.pdf
[2] Validating locational marginal emissions models with wind generation ,
https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/2753-3751/ad72f6/pdf
[3] Sofia, Sarah, and Yury Dvorkin.
"Carbon Impact of Intra-Regional Transmission Congestion." CellReports Sustainability, https://www.cell.com/action/showPdf?pii=S2949-7906%2825%2900273-3

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text:
Build margin methods must reflect financing, permitting, and transmission constraints observed in real markets. I align with suggestions from the ZeroGrid Impact Advisory Initiative, which specify the need for a standardized approach with observable data to limit confusion and manipulation. [1] Using observed data, rather than modeled, allows for increased accuracy within the model.

Methods assuming frictionless capacity expansion or ignoring transmission constraints. Under capacity expansion models, the answer is highly variable as it is based on differing inputs. For example, assuming frictionless build responses and materially misstate impacts under current demand, interconnection and permitting constraints,

For example, the ZeroGrid Impact Advisory Initiative (IAI)'s Performance Metric Principles, which focus primarily on maximizing emissions impact from and outside of renewable procurement, states: "Consequential assessment can be conducted using a variety of approaches, including capacity expansion models, yet these approaches are often complex, time-intensive, and subject to producing variable results based upon key inputs and assumptions." [1]

answers.text:
Hourly, nodal granularity is essential for measuring the marginal emissions impact at the
generator/facility level and capturing accurate congestion impacts. If nodal is not available, zonal or balancing authority can be used. Refer to MER hierarchy as proposed by the TWG on page 2 of this table: (https://marginalimpactmethod.org/Appendix_Table.pdf)

Assessing these impacts at the node allows for the highest credibility and accuracy associated with the total emissions impact claims as a result. Experts agree:

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text:
Higher temporal granularity improves accuracy and MERs should be as granular as possible given available data. Where hourly data are not available, annual would be better than no data. Refer to MER hierarchy as proposed by the TWG on page 2 of this table: https://marginalimpactmethod.org/Appendix_Table.pdf

The most appropriate temporal granularity for emission factors is the smallest interval for which accurate data is available, and marginal emissions rates vary materially hour-to-hour due to diurnal and seasonal variations, as well as from impacts of congestion.

1. Enhanced Accuracy and Alignment with Grid Operations
The core defense of hourly rates is that they accurately reflect the high frequency of changes in electricity generation and instantaneous grid dispatch. It is typically preferable to use hourly data or finer temporal granularity, as coarser data (e.g., annual) degrades the accuracy of the analysis due to diurnal and seasonal variations in marginal emissions rates.

2. Preventing Misestimation: Relying on coarse accounting methods, such as annual averages, can lead to wildly inaccurate estimates of carbon emissions, potentially over- or under-estimating emissions. This gap is expected to increase as renewables saturate the grid, making hourly measurements necessary for accurate accounting.

3. GHGP Recommendation: For the Location-Based Method (LBM) in GHG Protocol revisions, the proposed hierarchy lists hourly as the most precise temporal granularity. I agree and suggest that the same precision apply to the consequential metric.

It is important that hourly is not mandated as a condition of valid impact accounting.

answers.label: Appropriate margin weighting approaches
selections: Default 0.50 build margin weight for all projects
GHG Protocol Guidelines for Quantifying GHG Reductions from Grid-connected Electricity Projects

answers.label: Why selected weighting approaches are appropriate
answers.text:
They balance accuracy with feasibility and avoid overfitting models. Transparent, default weighting with flexibility for regional customization and both support default build/operating margin weights as a necessary simplification for scalability. Bespoke weighting materially reduces comparability and increases reporting cost without commensurate gains in accuracy. In addition, many of the approaches other assumed incorrectly suppressed demand and overcapacity (for example, the UNFCCC) which is clearly not the current grid situation.

I agree with WattTime [1] that the 50/50 weighting offers a feasible and defensible default option. This is being further researched by the VERACI-T group, and I expect that additional research will be available to further defend or amend this default case prior to the GHGP’s publication of the final rules in 2027.

As more research is done, it may become viable and advisable to develop a schedule of weights, where there is a different default rate based on different scenarios (region, project type, etc.) as detailed in the GHG Protocol Guidelines for Quantifying GHG Reductions from Grid-connected Electricity Projects. But it is worth noting that the pursuit of additional project-specific accuracy should be weighed against the goals of feasibility and comparability.

[1] How to use the GHG Protocol’s consequential electricity emissions reporting option https://watttime.org/news-and-insights/how-to-use-the-ghg-protocols-optional-consequential-electricity-emissions-reporting-option/

answers.label: Weighting approaches not feasible to implement
Why selected weighting approaches are infeasible
answers.text:
While all are feasible, some require excessive data, use inaccurate assumptions (like demand address in question 48 for UNFCCC), reduce comparability, and increase reporting burden.

The UNFCCC CDM methodology is a feasible option, but it is worth noting that it should be further researched what error is introduced when assume a default weighting of 0.75 OM/ 0.25 BM for all solar and wind projects (recommended by UNFCCC [1]), as compared to the 0.5 weighting.

The other two suggestions from the TWG (d. Resource adequacy approaches e. Intervention lifecycle approaches) could potentially be valid approaches, but I need more information about these approaches before being able to determine the feasibility of them.

[1] https://cdm.unfccc.int/methodologies/PAmethodologies/tools/am-tool-07-v7.0.pdf

answers.label: Other approaches for assigning margin weights
answers.text: Simplified dynamic weighting updated periodically based on observed grid trends.

answers.label: Research supporting the suggested approach
answers.text:
It is important to understand that much of the research supporting 24x7, deliverability and additionality was conducted using data from prior to 2020, a period of largely flat to negative U.S. load growth which did not consider the changes in the electrical demand from Artificial intelligence which could be as high as 3% per year or the equivalent of a 25% load growth over a 7 year period. (https://www.icf.com/insights/energy/electricity-demand-expected-to-grow?utm)

In addition, political changes, especially in the U.S., have negatively impacted tax credits, permitting policies and general political approach to renewables. Finally, power prices have risen materially (World Resources Institute (2025), What's Really Driving Up US Electricity Prices? We Unpack the Numbers. https://www.wri.org/insights/whats-driving-us-electricity-prices.

It is important for the GHGP to consider the impact of these changes in setting the new rules. The assumption under the original research of a centrally planned, frictionless electricity system where additional load or procurement trigger new clean generation, with perfect foresight and no capital or transmission constraints is not accurate and thus that research should not be relied upon.

For further insights into marginal emissions see Veraci-t dives deep into marginal emission rates. https://veraci-t.org/#section-106-9
